mainTopic: Blood absorbed in roasted and soaked meat: כבולעו כך פולטו, breaded and stuffed meat, meat on coals, and soaking in vinegar
overview: This amud opens with the last words of a rejected proof: in that case the blood has an open path and simply drips out. The גמרא then tries to support רבה's principle of כבולעו כך פולטו (as food absorbs, so it releases) from a משנה about roasting a heart. That proof is pushed away because the heart is smooth. Two stories, one about רב and a dove wrapped in dough and one about רבא and a breaded goose, are each explained by the type of flour used. This leads to a three-part הלכה for breaded meat, and to the ruling that stuffed meat (מולייתא) is permitted even with the opening facing up. Next comes a set of arguments between רב אחא and רבינא about raw meat, testicles and neck veins. They are permitted after salting or roasting on a spit, and also on coals, because the heat draws the blood out. The amud closes with raw meat soaked in vinegar: whether the vinegar's color matters, and why vinegar used once for soaking is not used again. That last answer continues on the next amud.

steps.title: There the blood simply drips out
steps.stepSummary: The tail end of an answer from the previous section: in that case the blood has a way out, so it drips away.
steps.simpleTranslation: It flows, it surely drips out.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing an answer it started on the previous amud. It explains that in the case being discussed, the blood has an opening and simply drips out.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This answer separates a case with an open path for the blood from regular stuffed meat (מולייתא), which is closed on all sides. When there is an opening, we do not need any special principle to explain why the food is permitted, because the blood just drains away by itself.

keyTerms.meaning: flowing, dripping (the doubled verb adds emphasis: it surely flows)
stuffed meat, closed on all sides (the background case on the previous amud)

steps.confusionAlert: This line is not a new teaching. It is the last two words of an answer that started on the previous amud, so do not read it as a standalone statement.

phrases.english: It surely flows out.
phrases.notes: Doubled verb for emphasis. It completes an answer from the previous section.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the rejection of an earlier proof for רבה's view on מולייתא, from the previous amud. That case had an open path for the blood, so it cannot prove anything about closed stuffing. The next step brings a new proof attempt.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Factual distinction: in this case there is a physical outlet for the blood.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We might have thought this case is like closed stuffing, where the blood is trapped.
steps.terutzMaskana: Here the blood has a path out and drips away, so it is not like closed stuffing.

steps.title: Trying to prove the absorb-and-release principle from the heart
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that a משנה about roasting a heart supports רבה's principle of כבולעו כך פולטו.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let us say this supports him: The heart must be torn open and its blood taken out. If he did not tear it, he tears it after cooking, and it is permitted. What is the reason? Is it not because we say that as it absorbs, so it releases?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a משנה and suggests it backs up רבה. The משנה says a heart roasted without being opened first is still permitted if you tear it open afterward.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A heart is full of blood, and roasting should push that blood into the meat. If the meat is still permitted, it seems the meat soaks up the blood and then pushes it back out during roasting. That is exactly רבה's rule of כבולעו כך פולטו.

keyTerms.meaning: Let us say it supports him (opens a proof attempt)
as it absorbs, so it releases
is it not because...? (a question that expects a yes)

steps.whyThisMatters: The principle of כבולעו כך פולטו is a basic tool in the laws of blood and absorbed flavors (בליעות). This step tests whether it can be proven from a משנה.

phrases.english: Let us say this supports him:
The heart: one tears it and removes its blood.

phrases.aramaic: לֹא קְרָעוֹ — קוֹרְעוֹ לְאַחַר בִּישּׁוּלוֹ, וּמוּתָּר.
phrases.english: If he did not tear it, he tears it after its cooking, and it is permitted.
What is the reason?
Is it not because we say
as it absorbs, so it releases?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the earlier back-and-forth to a new attempt to support רבה from a משנה.
steps.raayaObject: רבה's principle that meat absorbing blood during roasting also releases it (כבולעו כך פולטו).
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה that a heart roasted without being torn may be torn afterward and is permitted.

steps.title: The heart is different because it is smooth
steps.stepSummary: The proof is rejected: the heart is smooth and hardly absorbs blood, so it proves nothing about other foods.
steps.simpleTranslation: The heart is different, because it is smooth.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes away the proof. The heart is a special case because its smooth surface does not soak up much blood.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The heart may be permitted simply because it barely absorbs blood at all, not because of כבולעו כך פולטו. So the משנה cannot show that other foods, which do absorb blood, will release it again.

keyTerms.meaning: is different (a classic way to reject a proof)

phrases.english: A heart is different, because it is smooth.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof brought in step 2.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Only rejects the proof. It does not say רבה's principle is wrong.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The heart is a unique case. It barely absorbs, so it cannot teach the general rule.

steps.title: Challenge from רב eating dough roasted around a dove
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the claim that we do not generally rely on absorb-and-release. רב was willing to eat dough roasted around a young dove.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is that so? But רבין סבא wrapped a young dove in dough for רב, and רב said to him: If its dough is good, give me some and I will eat!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions the idea that, apart from the smooth heart, we cannot rely on כבולעו כך פולטו. It tells a story in which רב was ready to eat dough that had been roasted around a bird.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The dough wrapped around the raw dove should have soaked up blood while roasting. If רב still wanted to eat it, it seems he held that the dough released the blood again. That would show כבולעו כך פולטו works even for ordinary foods.

keyTerms.meaning: he coated or wrapped it (in dough)

phrases.english: (Is that so?) But surely רבין the Elder wrapped in dough
phrases.notes: The word in brackets is a textual variant.

phrases.english: a certain young dove for רב,
and he said to him:
If its dough is good,
give me and I will eat!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the position from step 3 that, aside from the smooth heart, we do not generally rely on absorb-and-release.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the absorb-and-release principle is not generally relied upon (only the heart is special).
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Dough around a roasting bird absorbs blood. רב's willingness to eat it suggests he held that the dough releases the blood, which is כבולעו כך פולטו in an ordinary food.

steps.title: The dough was crumbly fine flour
steps.stepSummary: The challenge is answered: that dough was made of crumbly fine flour, which lets the blood drain right through.
steps.simpleTranslation: That case was with fine flour that crumbles.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. The dough in רב's story was made of crumbly fine flour, so the blood simply drained through it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The dough was permitted because it was porous, not because of כבולעו כך פולטו. This matches the idea from step 1: when blood has a way out, it drips away. A tight, closed coating would be different.
steps.whatToRemember: Every proof for כבולעו כך פולטו here is set aside with a physical distinction. The heart is smooth and barely absorbs, and crumbly flour dough lets the blood drain out. Neither case forces us to rely on the general principle.

phrases.english: That one was with fine flour that crumbles.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 4.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Factual distinction about the material: crumbly fine flour.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We might have thought רב relied on the dough releasing the blood it absorbed.
steps.terutzMaskana: The crumbly dough let the blood flow through, so there is no proof for the general principle.

steps.title: רבא would only eat breaded goose if the coating stayed white
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges כבולעו כך פולטו from a story about רבא. He ate breaded goose only because the breading stayed clean white, which suggests breading can hold on to blood.
steps.simpleTranslation: But רבא once visited the house of the ריש גלותא, and they served him a young goose coated in dough. He said: 'If I had not seen that the coating was as clear as a shiny white coin, I would not have eaten it.' If you really think 'as it absorbs, so it releases,' why did it matter that the coating was clear? Even if it was not clear, it should be fine!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a story about רבא that seems to go against the rule of כבולעו כך פולטו.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the coating always lets out whatever blood it soaks up, its color should not matter. Yet רבא checked that it stayed white before eating. That suggests the coating can keep the blood inside, which challenges the rule.

keyTerms.meaning: The Exilarch, leader of the Jewish community in Babylonia
They coated or breaded (wrapped the meat in dough)
Shiny and clear like a new white coin
As it absorbs, so it releases

phrases.aramaic: וְהָא רָבָא אִיקְּלַע לְבֵי רֵישׁ גָּלוּתָא
phrases.english: But didn't Rava happen to come to the house of the Exilarch
and they coated a young goose in dough for him,
he said: If I had not seen it
that it was clear like a white coin,
I would not have eaten from it.
And if you think 'as it absorbs, so it releases',
why does it matter specifically when it is clear?
Even when it is not clear, it should also be allowed!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָא רָבָא אִיקְּלַע לְבֵי רֵישׁ גָּלוּתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new challenge pointing the opposite way from step 4. Step 4 attacked the claim that we cannot rely on כבולעו כך פולטו. This story attacks the principle itself, since רבא's caution implies that a coating can keep the blood it absorbed.
steps.kashyaTarget: The principle of כבולעו כך פולטו
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבא's need to check the coating's color shows that a coating can trap blood. That would not be true if everything absorbed is always released.

steps.title: רבא's coating was firm white flour
steps.stepSummary: The answer: רבא's coating was made of firm white flour, which does not let blood pass through. So he had to check it.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, it was firm white flour.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by pointing to the type of flour in רבא's case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Firm white flour is dense, so blood that goes in cannot drain out. That is why רבא needed to see the coating stay white. The story says nothing about ordinary or crumbly flour, so the principle stays standing.

phrases.english: There it was white flour, which is firm.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 6
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the case (אוקימתא) to a specific type of flour
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבא's caution shows that coatings in general trap blood
steps.terutzMaskana: Firm white flour does not let blood pass through, so רבא had to check that it stayed white. His caution says nothing against the principle for other coatings.
steps.confusionAlert: Notice the contrast with step 5. There the flour was crumbly fine flour (סמידא), which lets blood drain out. Here it is firm white flour, which holds blood in. The type of flour is what decides the case.

steps.title: Final rule for three kinds of breading
steps.stepSummary: The הלכה for meat coated in dough depends on the flour: fine flour is always permitted, white flour only if it stays white, and other flours only if they did not turn red.
steps.simpleTranslation: The הלכה is: a coating of fine flour is permitted whether it turned red or not. A coating of white flour is permitted if it is clear like a white coin, and forbidden if not. A coating of other flours is forbidden if it turned red, and permitted if it did not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sums up the practical law for coated meat, based on the two answers just given.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Fine flour (סמידא) is crumbly, so blood drains out and even redness does not matter. Firm white flour holds blood, so it must stay perfectly clean. Other flours fall in the middle, and redness is the sign that blood stayed inside.
steps.whatToRemember: Fine flour: always permitted. White flour: only if it stays shiny white. Other flour: permitted unless it turned red.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the practical bottom line for coated or breaded meat that is roasted with its blood.

phrases.english: And the law is: a coating of fine flour,

phrases.aramaic: בֵּין אַסְמֵיק בֵּין לָא אַסְמֵיק — שַׁרְיָא.
phrases.english: whether it turned red or did not turn red, is permitted.

phrases.aramaic: דְּחִיוָּרְתָּא, אִי זִיג כְּזוּזָא חִיוָּרָא — שַׁרְיָא,
phrases.english: A coating of white flour, if it is clear like a white coin, is permitted;
if not, it is forbidden.
A coating of other flours: if it turned red, it is forbidden;
if it did not turn red, it is permitted.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns the two answers about flour types into a final ruling
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Coated meat is judged by the type of flour and by whether the coating shows blood.

steps.title: How far each side goes on stuffed meat
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא returns to the argument about מוליתא (meat stuffed inside an animal). The one who forbids it does so even when the opening faces down, and the one who permits it does so even when the opening faces up.
steps.simpleTranslation: About this stuffed meat: the one who forbids it, forbids even if the opening faces down. The one who permits it, permits even if the opening faces up.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains how far each side of the מוליתא argument goes. This sets up the final ruling in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An opening facing down lets blood drip out, which should help. Even so, the one who forbids still forbids. An opening facing up keeps blood inside, which should hurt. Even so, the one who permits still permits. So the argument is about the principle itself, not about the position of the opening.

keyTerms.meaning: Stuffing: meat stuffed inside an animal and roasted

phrases.english: This stuffed meat,
the one who forbids it forbids even if the opening faces down,
and the one who permits it permits even if the opening faces up.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the original argument between אביי and רבה about stuffed meat, which was the source of the כבולעו כך פולטו discussion
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The argument applies no matter which way the opening faces.

steps.title: Stuffed meat is permitted even with the opening up
steps.stepSummary: The הלכה follows the lenient view: מוליתא is permitted even when the opening faces up.
steps.simpleTranslation: The הלכה is: stuffed meat is permitted, even if the opening faces up.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the final ruling on stuffed meat.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ruling follows רבה's view, based on כבולעו כך פולטו. Even the hardest case, where blood cannot drip out, is permitted.
steps.whatToRemember: Stuffed meat roasted together is permitted in every case, because whatever blood it absorbs it also releases.

phrases.english: And the law is: stuffed meat is permitted,
even if the opening faces up.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Decides the argument explained in step 9
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The הלכה follows the lenient view, based on כבולעו כך פולטו.

steps.title: Three meat cases argued by רב אחא and רבינא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא lists three cases of meat and blood that רב אחא and רבינא argue about: raw meat, testicles, and neck veins.
steps.simpleTranslation: Raw meat, testicles, and neck veins: רב אחא and רבינא argue about them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic by naming three cases and the two אמוראים who argue about them. This sets up the rule for deciding between them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: All three cases involve blood that may still be inside the meat. The גמרא does not say here who holds which view. That gap is filled in the next steps.

keyTerms.meaning: Large blood vessels of the neck

phrases.english: Raw meat, testicles, and neck veins,
Rav Acha and Ravina disagree about it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אוּמְצָא, בֵּיעֵי, וּמִיזְרְקֵי, פְּלִיגִי בַּהּ רַב אַחָא וְרָבִינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new, related topic about blood in meat
steps.mimraCoreRuling: There is an argument about three cases; no ruling is given yet.

steps.title: The usual rule: רב אחא is strict, רבינא is lenient
steps.stepSummary: Everywhere in the Torah where these two argue, רב אחא is strict, רבינא is lenient, and the הלכה follows רבינא.
steps.simpleTranslation: Throughout the whole Torah, רב אחא is strict and רבינא is lenient, and the הלכה follows רבינא, leniently.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a general rule for all arguments between רב אחא and רבינא. This prepares for the exception that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When we don't know who said what, we assume רב אחא took the strict view and רבינא the lenient one. We then rule like רבינא.

keyTerms.meaning: In the whole Torah, meaning in all of their arguments

phrases.english: In the whole Torah,
Rav Acha is strict and Ravina is lenient,
and the law follows Ravina, leniently.

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּכׇל הַתּוֹרָה כּוּלָּהּ רַב אַחָא לְחוּמְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the general rule for their arguments as background for the three cases
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In general, the הלכה follows the lenient רבינא.

steps.title: In these three cases the roles flip
steps.stepSummary: In the three cases (raw meat, testicles, neck veins), רב אחא is lenient and רבינא is strict, and the הלכה follows the lenient רב אחא.
steps.simpleTranslation: Except for these three, where רב אחא is lenient and רבינא is strict, and the הלכה follows רב אחא, leniently.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא names the exception to the usual rule and gives the final ruling for these three cases.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The names switch sides, but the outcome stays the same: the הלכה still follows the lenient view. In these three meat cases, that lenient view belongs to רב אחא.
steps.whatToRemember: The rule is always to be lenient. Usually that means ruling like רבינא, but in raw meat, testicles, and neck veins it means ruling like רב אחא.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't memorize 'the הלכה is always like רבינא.' In these three cases the lenient one is רב אחא, and the הלכה follows him.

phrases.english: Except for these three,
where Rav Acha is lenient and Ravina is strict,
and the law follows Rav Acha, leniently.

steps.triggerLanguage: לְבַר מֵהָנֵי תְּלָת דְּרַב אַחָא לְקוּלָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the exception to the general rule in step 12
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: In raw meat, testicles, and neck veins, the הלכה is lenient, following רב אחא.

steps.title: Raw meat that is salted or roasted on a spit is permitted
steps.stepSummary: Red raw meat (אומצא) that was cut and salted may even go into a pot. If roasted on a spit it is permitted, because the blood drips out.
steps.simpleTranslation: A piece of raw meat that is red with blood: if you cut it and salted it, you may even cook it in a pot. If you put it on a spit to roast, it is permitted, because the blood drips out.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins explaining the first of the three cases from Step 11, raw meat (אומצא). It first lists the two easy situations, where everyone agrees it is permitted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Salting pulls the blood out, so the meat may then be cooked in a pot. Roasting on a spit also works, because the blood simply drips down and away. These two cases are agreed on, so they set the background for the argument about coals in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: It flows out (the blood drips away)

phrases.english: This raw meat that became red,
if one cut it and salted it —
it is permitted even for a pot.
phrases.notes: Salting removes the blood, so it may then be cooked.

phrases.english: if one put it on a spit — it is permitted,
because the blood flows out.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts explaining the first case (raw meat) from the list in Steps 11 and 13.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Raw meat that is salted may be cooked in a pot, and raw meat roasted on a spit is permitted because the blood drips out.

steps.title: Argument about raw meat placed directly on coals
steps.stepSummary: If the raw meat is put on coals, רב אחא and רבינא argue. One forbids it because the coals shrivel the meat and trap the blood. One permits it because the heat sucks the blood out.
steps.simpleTranslation: If one put it on coals, רב אחא and רבינא argue about it: one forbids and one permits. The one who forbids holds that the meat shrivels and locks the blood in. The one who permits holds that the heat draws the blood out.
steps.whatsHappening: Now the גמרא reaches the case that is argued about: raw meat placed straight onto hot coals.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both sides agree on the facts but disagree about what the coals do to the meat. The strict view says the coals harden the outside so the blood cannot escape. The lenient view says the strong heat pulls the blood out of the meat.

keyTerms.meaning: It draws out (the heat sucks the blood out)

steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא does not say here who holds which view. From Step 13 we already know that in these three cases רב אחא is the lenient one and רבינא is the strict one, the opposite of their usual pattern.

phrases.english: if one placed it on coals —
Rav Acha and Ravina disagree about it,
one forbids and one permits.
The one who forbids holds that it shrivels.
And the one who permits holds that it draws out.
phrases.notes: The heat pulls the blood out.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַחֲתֵיהּ אַגּוּמְרֵי — פְּלִיגִי בַּהּ רַב אַחָא וְרָבִינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the agreed cases (salting and spit), presents the argued case of coals.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Raw meat on coals is argued about: forbidden if the coals trap the blood, permitted if they draw it out.

steps.title: The ruling: the coals draw out the blood
steps.stepSummary: The הלכה is that the coals draw the blood out, so raw meat placed on coals is permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the הלכה is: the heat draws the blood out.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא decides the argument about raw meat on coals in favor of the lenient view.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This fits Step 13, where we were told that in these three cases the הלכה follows the lenient view. Raw meat roasted directly on coals is permitted.

phrases.english: And the halacha is: it draws out.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Decides the argument from Step 15.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Raw meat placed on coals is permitted, because the heat draws the blood out.

steps.title: Same pattern for testicles
steps.stepSummary: Testicles (ביעי) follow the same pattern as raw meat. Salting allows a pot, a spit is permitted, and coals are argued about for the same two reasons.
steps.simpleTranslation: So too testicles: if you cut and salted them, you may even cook them in a pot. If you hung them on a spit, they are permitted, because the blood drips out. If you put them on coals, רב אחא and רבינא argue: one forbids and one permits. The one who forbids holds that they shrivel, and the one who permits holds that the heat draws the blood out.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the second case from the list, testicles, and repeats the same three-part pattern.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Nothing new is argued here. The same rules and the same reasons as for raw meat simply apply to testicles. The final ruling for this case is not stated again, but Step 13 already told us the הלכה follows the lenient view.

keyTerms.meaning: And so too (the same rule applies)

phrases.english: And so too testicles,
if one cut them and salted them —
they are permitted even for a pot.
if one hung them on a spit — they are permitted,
because the blood flows out.
if one placed them on coals —
Rav Acha and Ravina disagree about it,
one forbids and one permits.
The one who forbids holds that it shrivels.
And the one who permits holds that it draws out.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the raw-meat pattern from Steps 14 and 15 to the second case, testicles.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Testicles follow the same rules as raw meat: salting and a spit are permitted, and coals are argued about.

steps.title: Same pattern for neck veins, with the cut facing down
steps.stepSummary: Neck veins (מיזרקי) also follow the pattern. On a spit they are permitted only when the slaughter cut faces downward so the blood can drip out. Coals are argued about for the same two reasons.
steps.simpleTranslation: So too neck veins: if you cut and salted them, you may even cook them in a pot. If you hung them on a spit with the slaughter cut facing down, they are permitted, because the blood drips out. If you put them on coals, רב אחא and רבינא argue: one forbids and one permits. The one who forbids holds that they shrivel, and the one who permits holds that the heat draws the blood out.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the third case from the list, the large neck veins, using the same pattern with one added detail about the spit.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Veins hold a lot of blood. So on a spit they are permitted only if the slaughter cut (בית השחיטה) faces downward, which lets the blood drain out. Otherwise the rules and the argument are the same as before.

keyTerms.meaning: The place where the animal was slaughtered (the cut)

phrases.english: And so too neck veins: if one cut it and salted it —
it is permitted even for a pot.
if one hung it on a spit,
with the slaughter cut facing down — it is permitted,
phrases.notes: The extra condition: the blood needs a way to drip out.

phrases.english: because the blood flows out.
if one placed it on coals —
Rav Acha and Ravina disagree,
one forbids and one permits.
The one who forbids holds that it shrivels.
And the one who permits holds that it draws out.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the same pattern to the third case and adds the condition that the cut must face down on a spit.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Neck veins on a spit are permitted only with the slaughter cut facing down. On coals they are argued about.

steps.title: Final ruling: the coals draw out the blood
steps.stepSummary: The הלכה is again that the heat draws the blood out, so placing these on coals is permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the הלכה is: the heat draws the blood out.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא closes the three cases by ruling once more like the lenient view.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This confirms Step 13: in all three cases the lenient view wins. Raw meat, testicles, and neck veins placed on coals are permitted.

keyTerms.meaning: And the practical ruling is (spelling variant of הילכתא)

steps.whatToRemember: For raw meat, testicles, and neck veins: salting allows cooking in a pot, a spit is permitted (veins need the cut facing down), and coals are also permitted, because the heat draws the blood out.

phrases.english: And the halacha is: it draws out.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Decides the argument stated in Step 18 and closes the three-case section.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: In all three cases, placing the item on coals is permitted because the heat draws out the blood.

steps.title: Raw meat soaked in vinegar: depends on whether the vinegar turned red
steps.stepSummary: If the vinegar (חלא) that raw meat is soaking in turns red, the meat is forbidden. If it did not turn red, the meat is permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: Raw meat whose vinegar became red is forbidden. If its vinegar did not become red, it is permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic about blood: raw meat that was soaked in vinegar.
steps.deeperAnalysis: People soaked raw meat in vinegar. Red vinegar shows that blood came out of the meat, which makes it forbidden. Clear vinegar shows that no blood came out, so the meat is permitted.

keyTerms.meaning: Its vinegar (the vinegar it soaked in)

phrases.english: This raw meat
whose vinegar became red — is forbidden.
If its vinegar did not become red — it is permitted.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new case about blood in meat, this time soaked in vinegar.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Raw meat soaked in vinegar is forbidden only if the vinegar turned red.

steps.title: רבינא forbids the meat even when the vinegar stays clear
steps.stepSummary: רבינא says the meat is forbidden even if the vinegar did not turn red, because there must be some streaks of blood in it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said: even if the vinegar did not become red, it is forbidden. It is impossible that there are no streaks of blood in it.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא disagrees with the rule just stated and takes a stricter position.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבינא does not trust the color test. He holds that some blood always comes out into the vinegar, even when you cannot see it, so the meat is always forbidden.

phrases.english: Ravina said:

phrases.aramaic: אֲפִילּוּ לָא אַסְמֵיק נָמֵי חַלְיֵיהּ — אֲסִיר,
phrases.english: even if its vinegar did not become red — it is forbidden,

phrases.aramaic: אִי אֶפְשָׁר דְּלֵית בֵּהּ שׁוּרְיָיקֵי דְּמָא.
phrases.english: it is impossible that it has no streaks of blood.

steps.triggerLanguage: רָבִינָא אָמַר: אֲפִילּוּ לָא אַסְמֵיק נָמֵי חַלְיֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a stricter opposing view to the rule in Step 20.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבינא, raw meat soaked in vinegar is always forbidden, because some blood must have come out.

steps.title: Practice shows the vinegar was drunk without concern
steps.stepSummary: מר בר אמימר tells רב אשי that his father drank such vinegar. Another version says רב אשי himself drank it. Either way, this shows a lenient practice against רבינא.
steps.simpleTranslation: מר בר אמימר said to רב אשי: My father used to drink it down in gulps. Some say: רב אשי himself used to drink it down in gulps.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings what a great rabbi actually did, to show that the strict view of רבינא was not followed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If a leading rabbi drank this vinegar, he clearly did not think it was full of forbidden blood. That supports the first, lenient rule: clear vinegar is permitted. The איכא דאמרי only changes who drank it, not the lesson.

keyTerms.meaning: Some say (another version of the story)

steps.whatToRemember: Raw meat soaked in vinegar is judged by the vinegar's color. רבינא forbids it in all cases, but great rabbis drank such vinegar, which supports the lenient approach.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ מָר בַּר אַמֵּימָר לְרַב אָשֵׁי:
phrases.english: Mar bar Ameimar said to Rav Ashi:
Father would gulp it down.
phrases.notes: His father, אמימר, drank the vinegar without worry.

phrases.english: Some say:

phrases.aramaic: רַב אָשֵׁי גּוּפֵיהּ מְגַמַּע לֵיהּ גַּמּוֹעֵי.
phrases.english: Rav Ashi himself would gulp it down.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ מָר בַּר אַמֵּימָר לְרַב אָשֵׁי: אַבָּא מְגַמַּע לֵיהּ גַּמּוֹעֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a practical story that pushes back against רבינא's strict view from Step 21.
steps.raayaObject: The lenient rule that clear vinegar, and meat soaked in it, is not considered forbidden blood.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The practice of אמימר (or of רב אשי himself), who drank such vinegar.

steps.title: Ameimar did not reuse vinegar for a second soaking
steps.stepSummary: מר בר אמימר tells רב אשי that his father אמימר used vinegar to soak meat only once. He would not soak meat in the same vinegar a second time.
steps.simpleTranslation: מר בר אמימר said to רב אשי: My father, with this vinegar that he soaked meat in one time, he would not soak meat in it again.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא reports a practice of אמימר: vinegar that was already used once for soaking meat (חליטה) was not used again.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Meat is soaked in sharp vinegar so the sharpness locks its blood inside. Then the blood does not come out and spread. The point here is that after one use, the vinegar is treated as no longer strong enough to do this job.

keyTerms.meaning: Soaked or scalded meat in vinegar so the blood is sealed in

steps.confusionAlert: This shifts the focus from Steps 20-22. There, the question was whether the soaked meat stays permitted, judged by the vinegar's color. Here, the question is about the vinegar itself: once it has been used, can it still do its job of keeping the blood inside fresh meat?

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ מָר בַּר אַמֵּימָר לְרַב אָשֵׁי:
phrases.english: Mar bar Ameimar said to Rav Ashi:
My father, this vinegar
in which he soaked meat one time,
he would not soak meat in it again.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ מָר בַּר אַמֵּימָר לְרַב אָשֵׁי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Same speakers as Step 22, but now about a new vinegar law: reusing vinegar for soaking.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Vinegar already used once for soaking meat is not used for soaking again.

steps.title: Why is used vinegar different from weak vinegar?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why used vinegar is unfit for soaking when we do soak meat in weak vinegar (חלא מתמהא).
steps.simpleTranslation: What is different about this from weak vinegar, which we do soak meat in?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a question about אמימר's practice. If weak vinegar is good enough, why isn't once-used vinegar good enough too?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Used vinegar looks like it is just weaker vinegar. But weak vinegar is used for soaking. So the גמרא wants to know what makes used vinegar worse than vinegar that is weak from the start.

phrases.english: What is different from weak vinegar
in which we do soak meat?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the logic of the practice reported in Step 23.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What makes once-used vinegar unfit when weak vinegar is fit for soaking.

steps.title: The answer begins: in weak vinegar, the sharpness is still there
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא starts to answer: 'There (with weak vinegar), it is present.' The sentence finishes on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: There (with weak vinegar), it is present...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins its answer to Step 24, and the answer continues past the end of this passage.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer contrasts the two cases. With weak vinegar, its sharpness is still present, even if mild. The next passage will finish the contrast: in used vinegar, the sharpness has already been used up by the first soaking.
steps.confusionAlert: This sentence is cut off. 'It is present' refers to the vinegar's sharpness, which the next passage names.

phrases.english: There, the [sharpness] is present
phrases.notes: The answer continues on the next amud.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins answering the question of Step 24.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Partial: weak vinegar still has its sharpness. The contrast with used vinegar is completed on the next amud.
